lessons.title: Multi-Digit Multiplication
lessons.description: Multiply two-digit by two-digit numbers using the standard algorithm!
lessons.content:
Now you'll multiply bigger numbers! The standard algorithm breaks multiplication into steps: multiply by the ones digit, multiply by the tens digit (shift one place left), then add the partial products together.

For 23 × 15: First multiply 23 × 5 = 115. Then multiply 23 × 10 = 230 (write it shifted one place to the left). Add: 115 + 230 = 345.

This method works for any size numbers! The key is being careful about place value and alignment when adding the partial products.
steps: Write numbers stacked vertically
Multiply the top number by the ones digit of the bottom number
Multiply the top number by the tens digit, but shift one place left
If there are more digits, continue shifting left
Add all partial products together
lessons.tip: Always estimate first! For 23 × 15, think: 20 × 15 = 300. So the answer should be around 300. Getting 345? Yes, that's reasonable. If you got 34,500, you'd know something went wrong!

quiz.q: What is 12 × 13?
What is 24 × 11?
What are the partial products of 21 × 13?
quiz.explanation: 21 × 3 = 63 and 21 × 10 = 210. These are the partial products.

quiz.q: Estimate: About how much is 38 × 22?
quiz.explanation: 38 ≈ 40 and 22 ≈ 20. 40 × 20 = 800, so the answer is around 800. (Actual: 836)

lessons.title: Long Division
lessons.description: Divide larger numbers using the long division steps!
lessons.formula:
Long Division Steps (DMSB):
D = Divide
M = Multiply
S = Subtract
B = Bring down
Example: 156 ÷ 4 = 39
lessons.content:
Long division is a systematic way to divide large numbers. Remember the steps: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down (DMSB). Repeat until there's nothing left to bring down!

For 156 ÷ 4: How many 4s in 15? (3, since 3 × 4 = 12). Write 3 on top. Subtract: 15 − 12 = 3. Bring down the 6 to make 36. How many 4s in 36? (9, since 9 × 4 = 36). Write 9. Subtract: 36 − 36 = 0. Answer: 39!

If there's a remainder at the end, write it next to the quotient. For example, 17 ÷ 3 = 5 R 2 (5 with remainder 2).
steps: Set up: dividend inside, divisor outside
DIVIDE: How many times does the divisor go into the first digit(s)?
MULTIPLY: Multiply the quotient digit by the divisor
SUBTRACT: Subtract from the dividend digits
BRING DOWN: Bring down the next digit and repeat

examples.title: 196 ÷ 7
examples.text: 7 goes into 19: 2 times (2×7=14). 19-14=5. Bring down 6: 56. 7 goes into 56: 8 times (8×7=56). 56-56=0. Answer: 28!

examples.title: 145 ÷ 3
examples.text: 3 goes into 14: 4 times (4×3=12). 14-12=2. Bring down 5: 25. 3 goes into 25: 8 times (8×3=24). 25-24=1. Answer: 48 R 1.

lessons.tip: Remember DMSB: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. Some students like the mnemonic 'Does McDonald's Sell Burgers?' Write it at the top of your paper until it becomes automatic!

quiz.q: What is 144 ÷ 12?
What is 156 ÷ 4?
What is 97 ÷ 5?
What does 'B' stand for in DMSB?
quiz.explanation: B = Bring down. After subtracting, bring down the next digit from the dividend.

lessons.title: Factors, Multiples, GCF & LCM
lessons.description: Find factors and multiples, and determine greatest common factors and least common multiples!
lessons.formula:
Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12
Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18...
GCF of 12 and 18 = 6
LCM of 4 and 6 = 12
lessons.content:
Factors are numbers that divide evenly into another number. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 (because each divides 12 with no remainder). Multiples are the products you get when you multiply a number. The multiples of 3 are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15...

The Greatest Common Factor (GCF) of two numbers is the largest number that divides both. For 12 and 18: factors of 12 are {1,2,3,4,6,12} and factors of 18 are {1,2,3,6,9,18}. The common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6 — so GCF = 6.

The Least Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest number that's a multiple of both. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16... Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18... The LCM is 12!
steps: To find factors: divide the number by 1, 2, 3... up to the number
To find multiples: multiply the number by 1, 2, 3...
For GCF: list ALL factors of both numbers, find the largest common one
For LCM: list multiples of both until you find one that matches
Prime numbers have exactly 2 factors (1 and itself)

examples.title: Finding LCM of 8 and 10
examples.text: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40... Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40... First match: 40. LCM = 40.

lessons.tip: To quickly find the GCF, list factors in pairs! For 24: (1,24), (2,12), (3,8), (4,6). Once pairs meet or cross, you've found all factors. This prevents missing any!

quiz.q: What are the factors of 16?
What is the GCF of 12 and 20?
quiz.explanation: Factors of 12: {1,2,3,4,6,12}. Factors of 20: {1,2,4,5,10,20}. Greatest common: 4.

quiz.q: What is the LCM of 3 and 5?
quiz.explanation: Multiples of 3: 3,6,9,12,15. Multiples of 5: 5,10,15. First common: 15.

quiz.q: Which number is prime?
quiz.explanation: 11 has exactly 2 factors: 1 and 11. That makes it prime!

lessons.title: Prime and Composite Numbers
lessons.description: Identify prime and composite numbers by finding factors.
lessons.formula:
Prime Number: has exactly 2 factors (1 and itself)
Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13...

Composite Number: has more than 2 factors
Examples: 4 (1,2,4), 6 (1,2,3,6), 8 (1,2,4,8)

Special: 1 is NEITHER prime nor composite
lessons.content:
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. The number 7 is prime because its only factors are 1 and 7. A composite number has more than two factors. The number 6 is composite because its factors are 1, 2, 3, and 6.

To determine if a number is prime or composite, list all its factor pairs. If you find more than one pair (besides 1 and itself), the number is composite. The number 1 is special — it is neither prime nor composite because it has only one factor. The number 2 is the only even prime number!
steps: Start with the number you want to test
List factor pairs: start with 1 x the number
Try 2: is the number divisible by 2? If yes, it is composite
Try 3, then 4, then 5... until you reach the number's square root
If no factors are found besides 1 and itself, the number is prime

examples.title: Is 13 Prime?
examples.text: Factors of 13: 1 x 13. Try 2: 13 ÷ 2 = 6.5 (no). Try 3: 13 ÷ 3 = 4.33 (no). Only factors are 1 and 13. So 13 is PRIME.

examples.title: Is 12 Composite?
examples.text: Factor pairs of 12: 1 x 12, 2 x 6, 3 x 4. It has 6 factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. More than 2 factors, so 12 is COMPOSITE.

lessons.tip: Quick divisibility tricks: if a number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, it is divisible by 2. If the digits add up to a multiple of 3, it is divisible by 3. If it ends in 0 or 5, it is divisible by 5. These shortcuts speed up factor finding!

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is prime?
quiz.explanation: 11 has only two factors: 1 and 11. It is prime. 9 (1,3,9), 15 (1,3,5,15), and 21 (1,3,7,21) are composite.

quiz.q: Is the number 1 prime, composite, or neither?
quiz.explanation: The number 1 has only one factor (itself). Since it does not have exactly 2 factors, it is neither prime nor composite.

quiz.q: What are all the factors of 10?
quiz.explanation: Factor pairs: 1 x 10 and 2 x 5. So the factors are 1, 2, 5, 10. Since it has 4 factors, 10 is composite.

lessons.title: Fraction Multiplication
lessons.description: Multiply a fraction by a whole number using models and equations.
lessons.formula:
Fraction x Whole Number:
   a         a x n
 --- x n = -------
   b           b

3 x 2/5 = (3 x 2)/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5
  (multiply the whole number by the numerator)

1/4 x 3 = 3/4
lessons.content:
Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is like repeated addition of that fraction. If you multiply 1/4 by 3, you are adding 1/4 three times: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. The rule is simple: multiply the whole number by the numerator, and keep the denominator the same.

Sometimes the product is an improper fraction (numerator bigger than denominator), like 3 x 2/3 = 6/3 = 2. You can convert improper fractions to mixed numbers or whole numbers by dividing. Using area models helps you visualize: shade 2/3 of a bar, three times, and see the total.
steps: Write the fraction next to the whole number
Multiply the whole number by the numerator (top)
Keep the denominator (bottom) the same
If the numerator is bigger than the denominator, simplify or convert to a mixed number
Check with a model: draw the fraction repeated that many times

examples.title: 2 x 3/8
examples.text: Multiply whole number by numerator: 2 x 3 = 6. Keep denominator: 6/8. Simplify: divide by 2 = 3/4. So 2 x 3/8 = 3/4.

examples.title: 4 x 1/3
examples.text: Multiply: 4 x 1 = 4. Keep denominator: 4/3. This is 1 1/3 as a mixed number. You have one whole plus one-third extra.

lessons.tip: Think of it as groups! 3 x 2/5 means '3 groups of 2/5.' Draw 3 bars, shade 2/5 of each bar, then count all the shaded pieces. You should see 6 out of 5 pieces total, which is 6/5 or 1 1/5.

quiz.q: What is 3 x 1/5?
quiz.explanation: Multiply 3 x 1 = 3 (numerator). Keep denominator: 3/5.

quiz.q: What is 2 x 3/4?
quiz.explanation: 2 x 3 = 6 (numerator). Keep denominator: 6/4. Simplify: 6/4 = 1 1/2.

quiz.q: What is 5 x 1/6?
quiz.explanation: 5 x 1 = 5 (numerator). Keep denominator: 5/6.

lessons.title: Prime Factorization and Factor Trees
lessons.description: Learn how to break numbers down into their prime factors using factor trees, and discover the difference between prime and composite numbers.
lessons.formula:
Every composite number can be written as a product of prime factors.

Example: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2³ × 3
lessons.content:
A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. The numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11 are all prime numbers because nothing divides them evenly except 1 and the number itself. A composite number is a whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors, meaning it can be broken down into smaller pieces. For example, 12 is composite because its factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12.

A factor tree is a handy tool that helps you find the prime factors of any composite number. To build one, start by writing your number at the top, then draw two branches downward to a pair of factors that multiply to give your number. Keep branching until every number at the bottom of your tree is prime — those bottom numbers are your prime factorization. You can check your work by multiplying all the prime factors together; the product should equal your original number.

Prime factorization is useful far beyond this lesson. It is the foundation for finding the greatest common factor (GCF) and the least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers, skills you will use when simplifying fractions and finding common denominators. The number 1 is special because it is neither prime nor composite, so always remember that prime numbers start at 2.
steps: Decide whether the number is prime or composite. If it has more than two factors, it is composite and can be factored further.
Write the composite number at the top of your factor tree.
Choose any factor pair of the number and draw two branches below it.
If either factor on the bottom is composite, repeat the branching process until every number at the bottom is prime.
Write the prime factorization by listing all the prime factors in order from smallest to largest.

examples.title: Factor Tree for 36
examples.text: Start with 36 at the top. Split into 6 × 6. Each 6 splits into 2 × 3. The prime factorization of 36 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, which can be written as 2² × 3². You can verify this by multiplying: 4 × 9 = 36.

examples.title: Factor Tree for 60
examples.text: Start with 60 at the top. Split into 6 × 10. The 6 splits into 2 × 3, and the 10 splits into 2 × 5. The prime factorization of 60 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 5, or 2² × 3 × 5. Check: 4 × 3 × 5 = 60.

lessons.tip: Always double-check your factor tree by multiplying all the prime factors back together. If the product does not match your original number, you made a mistake somewhere in the branches!

quiz.q: What is the prime factorization of 28?
quiz.explanation: The prime factorization of 28 is 2 × 2 × 7. We can find this by splitting 28 into 4 × 7, then splitting 4 into 2 × 2.

quiz.q: Which number in the list below is composite?
quiz.explanation: 27 is composite because its factors are 1, 3, 9, and 27. The other numbers are all prime since they have no factors other than 1 and themselves.

quiz.q: What is the prime factorization of 48?
quiz.explanation: The prime factorization of 48 is 2⁴ × 3. We can find this by splitting 48 into 6 × 8, then 6 into 2 × 3, and 8 into 2 × 2 × 2, giving us 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3.

quiz.q: What are the factors of the prime number 13?
quiz.explanation: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. The number 13 has no other factors because it cannot be divided evenly by any number other than 1 and 13.

lessons.title: Decimals: Tenths & Hundredths
lessons.description: Understand decimal numbers as tenths and hundredths!
lessons.formula:
Decimal Place Values:
0.3 = three tenths = 3/10
0.37 = three tenths + seven hundredths
0.37 = 37/100
0.3 = 0.30 = 30/100
lessons.content:
Decimals are a way to write numbers that are less than 1 — or the fractional part of a number. The decimal point separates the whole number part from the fractional part. The first digit after the point is tenths (10ths), and the second is hundredths (100ths).

0.3 means 'three tenths' which equals 3/10. 0.37 means 'thirty-seven hundredths' which equals 37/100. Just like place value with whole numbers, each position is worth 10 times more than the one to its right.

Decimals connect fractions to our base-10 number system. 1/10 = 0.1, 1/4 = 0.25, 1/2 = 0.5, 3/4 = 0.75. Money uses decimals too — $1.25 is 1 dollar and 25 cents!
steps: The decimal point separates whole numbers from fractions
First digit after decimal = tenths place (÷10)
Second digit = hundredths place (÷100)
To convert tenths to hundredths: multiply by 10 (0.3 = 0.30)
To compare decimals: line up the decimal points and compare digit by digit

examples.title: Understanding 0.47
examples.text: 0.47 = 4 tenths + 7 hundredths = 40/100 + 7/100 = 47/100. The 4 is worth 0.4 and the 7 is worth 0.07.

examples.title: Comparing 0.3 and 0.27
examples.text: Line up: 0.30 vs 0.27. Compare tenths: 3 > 2, so 0.30 > 0.27. Even though 27 looks bigger than 3, 0.3 > 0.27!

lessons.tip: When comparing decimals, always add a zero to make the same number of decimal places! Compare 0.30 vs 0.27 instead of 0.3 vs 0.27. This makes it clear that 0.3 is actually larger!

quiz.q: What is 3 tenths as a decimal?
quiz.explanation: 3 tenths = 3/10 = 0.3. The 3 is in the tenths place.

quiz.q: Which is larger: 0.42 or 0.5?
quiz.explanation: Compare as 0.42 vs 0.50. The tenths digit: 4 < 5, so 0.50 > 0.42.

quiz.q: What fraction equals 0.25?
quiz.explanation: 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4. Twenty-five cents is a quarter of a dollar!

quiz.q: What place value is the 8 in 0.86?
quiz.explanation: The 8 is the first digit after the decimal point, so it's in the tenths place.

lessons.title: Equivalent Fractions & Comparing
lessons.description: Find equivalent fractions and compare fractions with different denominators!
lessons.formula:
Equivalent Fractions:
Multiply top and bottom by same number
1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8
Comparing:
Use common denominator or cross-multiply
lessons.content:
Equivalent fractions look different but represent the same amount! 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8. They're all equal! You create equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing both the numerator and denominator by the same number.

To compare fractions with different denominators, find a common denominator — rewrite both fractions so they have the same denominator. Then compare the numerators.

For example, to compare 2/5 and 3/8: Common denominator = 40. Rewrite: 2/5 = 16/40 and 3/8 = 15/40. Since 16 > 15, we know 2/5 > 3/8.
steps: To find equivalent fractions: multiply or divide both top and bottom by the same number
To compare: find a common denominator (LCM of the denominators works)
Convert both fractions to the common denominator
Compare the numerators (larger numerator = larger fraction)
Simplify fractions by dividing numerator and denominator by their GCF

examples.title: Finding Equivalent Fractions
examples.text: Find a fraction equal to 3/4 with denominator 12. 4 × 3 = 12, so multiply both by 3: 3/4 = 9/12.

lessons.tip: Cross-multiplication is a quick way to compare two fractions! For a/b vs c/d, compute a×d and b×c. If a×d > b×c, then a/b > c/d. For 2/5 vs 3/8: 2×8 = 16 and 5×3 = 15. Since 16 > 15, 2/5 > 3/8.

quiz.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/3?
quiz.explanation: Multiply 1/3 by 2/2: 1×2/3×2 = 2/6. They're equivalent!

quiz.q: Which is larger: 2/3 or 3/5?
Simplify 8/12 to lowest terms.
quiz.explanation: GCF of 8 and 12 is 4. Divide both by 4: 8÷4/12÷4 = 2/3.

quiz.q: What common denominator would you use for 1/4 and 2/3?

lessons.title: Fraction Addition and Subtraction
lessons.description: Add and subtract fractions with like denominators using models.
lessons.formula:
Adding Fractions (same denominator):
  a   c   a + c
 --- + --- = -----
  n   n     n

1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5
  (add numerators only, keep denominator)

3/8 - 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4
lessons.content:
When fractions have the same denominator (called like denominators), adding and subtracting is straightforward. You add or subtract only the numerators while keeping the denominator the same. For example, 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. Think of it as combining pieces that are the same size.

Always check if your answer can be simplified. If both the numerator and denominator share a common factor, divide both by that factor. For example, 2/8 can be simplified to 1/4 by dividing top and bottom by 2. With models, you can see that 2 out of 8 equal sections is the same as 1 out of 4.
steps: Check that both fractions have the same denominator
Add or subtract the numerators (top numbers)
Keep the denominator the same
Simplify the answer if possible (divide both by a common factor)
Check with a model: does your answer make sense visually?

examples.title: Adding: 3/10 + 4/10
examples.text: Same denominator (10). Add numerators: 3 + 4 = 7. Answer: 7/10. This cannot be simplified further.

examples.title: Subtracting: 5/6 - 2/6
examples.text: Same denominator (6). Subtract numerators: 5 - 2 = 3. Answer: 3/6. Simplify: divide both by 3 to get 1/2. So 5/6 - 2/6 = 1/2.

lessons.tip: Remember: you NEVER add or subtract denominators! The denominator tells you the size of the pieces, and that does not change. You only combine or remove pieces (numerators). Think of it like this: 2 slices of an 8-slice pizza + 3 slices = 5 slices of an 8-slice pizza!

quiz.q: What is 1/4 + 2/4?
quiz.explanation: Same denominator. Add numerators: 1 + 2 = 3. Answer: 3/4.

quiz.q: What is 7/9 - 4/9?
quiz.explanation: Same denominator. Subtract: 7 - 4 = 3. Answer: 3/9. Simplify to 1/3. Both are correct.

quiz.q: What is 3/5 + 1/5?
quiz.explanation: Same denominator. Add numerators: 3 + 1 = 4. Answer: 4/5.

lessons.title: Decimal Operations
lessons.description: Add, subtract, and compare decimals to the hundredths place.
lessons.formula:
Decimal Place Value:
  3  .  4  7
ones . tenths hundredths
3 = 3 ones, .4 = 4 tenths, .07 = 7 hundredths

Comparing Decimals:
0.45 < 0.52 (compare tenths first, then hundredths)

Adding: 1.3 + 2.45 = 3.75
  Line up the decimal points!
lessons.content:
Decimals are a way to write numbers that include parts of a whole. The decimal point separates the whole number part from the fractional part. The first digit after the decimal point is the tenths place (worth 1/10), and the second digit is the hundredths place (worth 1/100). For example, 0.35 means 3 tenths and 5 hundredths.

When adding or subtracting decimals, the most important rule is to line up the decimal points. This ensures that you add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths. When comparing decimals, compare digit by digit from left to right, just like whole numbers. A longer decimal is not always bigger — 0.5 is larger than 0.49!
steps: Identify the place value of each digit (tenths, hundredths)
For comparing: line up decimals and compare from left to right
For adding/subtracting: stack numbers and line up the decimal points
Add or subtract column by column, starting from the right
Bring the decimal point straight down into your answer

examples.title: Comparing: 0.62 vs 0.59
examples.text: Line up: 0.62 and 0.59. Compare tenths: 6 > 5. So 0.62 > 0.59, even though 59 as a whole number is bigger!

examples.title: Adding: 3.45 + 2.3
examples.text: Write as 3.45 + 2.30 (add a zero). Add: hundredths: 5 + 0 = 5. Tenths: 4 + 3 = 7. Ones: 3 + 2 = 5. Answer: 5.75.

lessons.tip: When comparing decimals, imagine filling in zeros to make them the same length. Compare 0.50 vs 0.49 by writing them as 0.50 and 0.49 — now it is clear that 50 hundredths is more than 49 hundredths!

quiz.q: Which is bigger: 0.7 or 0.69?
quiz.explanation: 0.70 vs 0.69. Compare tenths: 7 > 6, so 0.7 > 0.69.

quiz.q: What is 2.5 + 1.37?
quiz.explanation: Line up: 2.50 + 1.37. Hundredths: 0+7=7. Tenths: 5+3=8. Ones: 2+1=3. Answer: 3.87.
Line up decimals. Subtract: borrow from tenths. 4.20 - 1.65 = 2.55.

lessons.title: Line Plots with Fractions
lessons.description: Create and interpret line plots using fractional measurement data.
lessons.formula:
Line Plot Example:
Lengths of pencils (in inches):

  X         X
  X   X     X
  X   X  X  X
--+---+--+--+--
 3/4 1 1 1/4 1 1/2

Each X = one item. Count X's to find frequency.
lessons.content:
A line plot is a graph that shows data on a number line. Each piece of data is represented by an X mark above the corresponding value. When measurements involve fractions, line plots are especially useful because you can see how the data is distributed across fractional values.

To read a line plot, count the X marks above each value. To find the total number of items, count all the X marks. To compare categories, see which value has the most or fewest X marks. Line plots make it easy to answer questions like 'how many objects measured more than 1/2 inch?' or 'what was the most common measurement?'
steps: Look at the scale along the bottom of the line plot (what numbers are shown)
Count the X marks above each value to find the frequency
To find the total, count ALL the X marks on the entire plot
To compare, identify which values have the most or least X marks
Answer questions by reading the X counts for specific values

examples.title: Reading a Line Plot
examples.text: A line plot shows plant heights: 1/4 has 2 X's, 1/2 has 5 X's, 3/4 has 3 X's, and 1 has 1 X. The most common height is 1/2 inch (5 plants). Total plants: 2 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 11.

examples.title: Answering Questions
examples.text: How many plants are taller than 1/2 inch? Count X's above 3/4 (3) and 1 (1): 3 + 1 = 4 plants are taller than 1/2 inch.

lessons.tip: When creating your own line plot, always include a title and labels! The scale should show all the values in your data set. If you have measurements of 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, and 1, make sure your number line includes all four marks.

quiz.q: On a line plot, 1/2 has 4 X's and 1/4 has 2 X's. How many more items measured 1/2?
quiz.explanation: 4 X's minus 2 X's = 2 more items measured 1/2 than 1/4.

quiz.q: A line plot has X's at 1/8 (3), 1/4 (4), 3/8 (2). What is the total number of items?
quiz.explanation: Total = 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 items.

quiz.q: Which value on a line plot is the mode (most frequent)?
options: The value with the most X's
The value with the fewest X's
quiz.explanation: The mode is the most common value, which on a line plot is the value with the most X marks above it.

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions with Unlike Denominators
lessons.description: Master finding common denominators using the least common multiple, converting fractions, and adding or subtracting fractions that have different bottom numbers.
lessons.formula:
To add or subtract fractions with unlike denominators:

1. Find the LCD of the denominators.
2. Convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction with the LCD.
3. Add or subtract the numerators; keep the denominator.

Example: 1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12
lessons.content:
When fractions have the same denominator, adding and subtracting is straightforward — you simply combine or separate the numerators while keeping the denominator unchanged. However, when two fractions have unlike denominators, you cannot add or subtract them directly because the pieces they describe are different sizes. Instead, you first need to find a common denominator, a new bottom number that both fractions can share.

The most efficient common denominator to use is the least common denominator (LCD), which is the least common multiple (LCM) of the two denominators. Once you have the LCD, you convert each original fraction into an equivalent fraction with the LCD as its new denominator. You do this by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the same number so the value of the fraction does not change. After both fractions share the same denominator, you add or subtract the numerators and write the result over the common denominator.

Always simplify your final answer if possible by dividing the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor. For example, if your answer is 6/8, you would simplify it to 3/4. Remember that you can never add or subtract denominators — only numerators. This skill is essential for working with measurements, recipes, and many real-world situations that involve fractional amounts.
steps: Identify the denominators of both fractions.
Find the least common multiple (LCM) of the denominators to get the LCD.
Convert the first fraction to an equivalent fraction with the LCD as the new denominator.
Convert the second fraction to an equivalent fraction with the LCD as the new denominator.
Add or subtract the numerators, keep the common denominator, and simplify the result.

examples.title: Adding 1/3 + 1/4
examples.text: The denominators are 3 and 4. The LCM of 3 and 4 is 12, so the LCD is 12. Convert 1/3 to 4/12 (multiply top and bottom by 4) and 1/4 to 3/12 (multiply top and bottom by 3). Now add: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12. The answer is already in simplest form.

examples.title: Subtracting 5/6 − 1/4
examples.text: The denominators are 6 and 4. The LCM of 6 and 4 is 12, so the LCD is 12. Convert 5/6 to 10/12 and 1/4 to 3/12. Now subtract: 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12. The fraction 7/12 cannot be simplified further, so this is the final answer.

lessons.tip: If you are struggling to find the LCD quickly, just multiply the two denominators together to get a common denominator. It may not be the least common denominator, but it will always work, and you can simplify at the end.

quiz.q: What is 2/5 + 1/3?
quiz.explanation: The LCD of 5 and 3 is 15. Convert 2/5 to 6/15 and 1/3 to 5/15. Adding: 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15.

quiz.q: What is 3/4 − 1/6?
quiz.explanation: The LCD of 4 and 6 is 12. Convert 3/4 to 9/12 and 1/6 to 2/12. Subtracting: 9/12 − 2/12 = 7/12.

quiz.q: What is the LCD of 8 and 12?
quiz.explanation: The multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, 32... and the multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36... The least common multiple is 24, so the LCD is 24.

quiz.q: What is 5/6 − 1/4?
quiz.explanation: The LCD of 6 and 4 is 12. Convert 5/6 to 10/12 and 1/4 to 3/12. Subtracting: 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12.

lessons.title: Decimals on a Number Line
lessons.description: Learn how to locate and plot tenths and hundredths accurately on a number line, and compare decimal values with confidence.
lessons.formula:
A decimal represents a fraction with a denominator of 10 or 100.

0.3 = 3/10 (three tenths)
0.07 = 7/100 (seven hundredths)
0.35 = 35/100 = 3 tenths and 5 hundredths
lessons.content:
Decimals are a way of writing numbers that fall between whole numbers, and a number line is one of the best tools for understanding exactly where a decimal belongs. When you look at a number line marked in tenths, each tick mark between two consecutive whole numbers represents one tenth. For example, between 0 and 1, the mark labeled 0.3 represents three tenths, or 3/10 of the way from 0 to 1.

When a number line is divided into hundredths, there are ten smaller spaces between each pair of tenth marks. The place to the right of the decimal point is the tenths place, and the next place to the right is the hundredths place. A number like 0.35 means three tenths and five hundredths, which is the same as 35/100. Understanding this place value system makes it easy to read, write, and compare decimals.

Comparing decimals is similar to comparing whole numbers: line up the decimal points and compare digit by digit from left to right. If two decimals have different numbers of digits after the decimal point, you can add a zero to the shorter one without changing its value. For example, 0.4 is the same as 0.40, and this makes it easy to see that 0.40 is greater than 0.35. Mastering decimals on a number line builds the visual understanding you need for measurement, money, and advanced math.
steps: Identify the two whole numbers that the decimal falls between.
Determine whether the number line is divided into tenths or hundredths.
Count the tick marks from the lower whole number to locate the decimal’s position.
For hundredths, first find the correct tenths mark, then count hundredths within that section.
Plot or label the decimal on the number line and verify by converting it to a fraction.

examples.title: Locating 0.47 on a Number Line
examples.text: The number 0.47 falls between 0 and 1. On a number line divided into tenths, first find the mark for 0.4. Between 0.4 and 0.5, count seven small marks to the right to reach 0.47, since the hundredths digit is 7.

examples.title: Comparing 0.52 and 0.6
examples.text: Line up the decimals: 0.52 and 0.60. Compare digit by digit: the tenths place has 5 vs 6. Since 5 < 6, we know 0.52 < 0.6. On a number line, 0.52 is to the left of 0.6.

lessons.tip: When comparing decimals, always write them with the same number of decimal places. Adding zeros to the end (like turning 0.6 into 0.60) makes it much easier to compare without making mistakes.

quiz.q: Where would 0.35 be located on a number line?
quiz.explanation: The number 0.35 is between 0.3 and 0.4. The tenths digit is 3, placing it in the section between 0.3 and 0.4, and the hundredths digit is 5, placing it halfway between those two marks.

quiz.q: Which decimal is the smallest?
quiz.explanation: Compare the tenths place first: 0.45 has 4 tenths, 0.09 has 0 tenths, 0.3 has 3 tenths, and 0.21 has 2 tenths. Since 0 tenths is the smallest, 0.09 is the least number.

quiz.q: What fraction is equivalent to 0.7?
quiz.explanation: The decimal 0.7 means 7 tenths, which is written as the fraction 7/10. Note that 70/1000 is not correct and 7/100 would be 0.07.

quiz.q: How many hundredths are in 0.63?
quiz.explanation: The decimal 0.63 is equal to 63 hundredths, or 63/100. The 6 is in the tenths place (6 tenths = 60 hundredths) and the 3 is in the hundredths place (3 hundredths), totaling 63 hundredths.

lessons.title: Simplifying Fractions to Lowest Terms
lessons.description: Reduce fractions to their simplest form by finding the Greatest Common Factor of the numerator and denominator.
lessons.formula:
To simplify: Find GCF of numerator and denominator, divide both by GCF.
4/8 → GCF(4,8)=4 → (4÷4)/(8÷4) = 1/2.

A fraction is in simplest form when GCF(numerator, denominator) = 1.
lessons.content:
Simplifying (or reducing) a fraction means rewriting it in its smallest possible form while keeping the same value. The fraction 4/8 and 1/2 represent the same amount — half of a whole — but 1/2 is the simplest form. To simplify, you find the Greatest Common Factor (GCF) of the numerator and denominator, then divide both by that number. Think of it like cutting a pizza into fewer, bigger slices that still cover the same area.

Here's how to find the GCF: list all the factors of the numerator and denominator, then pick the largest one they share. For 6/9, the factors of 6 are {1, 2, 3, 6} and the factors of 9 are {1, 3, 9}. The GCF is 3. Divide both numbers by 3: (6÷3)/(9÷3) = 2/3. You can also use a shortcut — if both numbers are even, divide by 2 first; if both end in 0 or 5, try 5. Keep dividing until the numerator and denominator share no common factors other than 1.

Why simplify? Simplified fractions are easier to understand and compare. Knowing that 12/16 equals 3/4 makes it clear that you have three-fourths of something. A fraction is fully simplified when the GCF of its numerator and denominator is 1 — meaning they have no common factors. Always double-check your work by multiplying back: (3 × 4) = 12 and (4 × 4) = 16, confirming that 3/4 = 12/16.
steps: Identify the numerator and denominator of the fraction
List the factors of both the numerator and the denominator
Find the Greatest Common Factor (GCF) — the largest factor they share
Divide both the numerator and denominator by the GCF
Verify: multiply back to confirm the simplified fraction equals the original

examples.title: Simplifying 6/9
examples.text: 6/9: Factors of 6 are {1,2,3,6}, factors of 9 are {1,3,9}. GCF = 3. Divide both by 3: (6÷3)/(9÷3) = 2/3. So 6/9 simplifies to 2/3.

examples.title: Simplifying 12/16
examples.text: 12/16: Factors of 12 are {1,2,3,4,6,12}, factors of 16 are {1,2,4,8,16}. GCF = 4. Divide both by 4: (12÷4)/(16÷4) = 3/4. So 12/16 simplifies to 3/4.

lessons.tip: Start by checking if both numbers are divisible by 2, 3, or 5 — these are the most common factors. Divide step by step until you can't divide anymore!

quiz.q: What is 4/8 in simplest form?
Simplify 10/15.
A fraction is in simplest form when:
options: GCF of numerator and denominator is 1
quiz.explanation: A fraction is fully simplified when the only common factor of the numerator and denominator is 1, meaning GCF = 1.

quiz.q: What is the GCF of 12 and 18?
quiz.explanation: Factors of 12: {1,2,3,4,6,12}. Factors of 18: {1,2,3,6,9,18}. The greatest common factor is 6.

lessons.title: Coordinate Plane Basics
lessons.description: Plot points and read coordinates on the first quadrant of the coordinate plane.
lessons.formula:
Coordinate Plane:
  Y
  5|  . (2,4)
  4|  .
  3|  .
  2|  .
  1|  .
   +---------- X
  0 1 2 3 4 5

Ordered Pair: (x, y)
(2, 4) means: go right 2, then up 4
lessons.content:
A coordinate plane is a grid formed by two number lines that cross at right angles. The horizontal line is the x-axis, and the vertical line is the y-axis. The point where they cross is called the origin and has coordinates (0, 0).

Every point on the plane is described by an ordered pair (x, y). The first number tells you how far to move left or right from the origin, and the second number tells you how far to move up or down. To plot (3, 2), start at the origin, go right 3, then go up 2. Always remember: over then up — x comes before y, just like in the alphabet!
steps: Start at the origin (0, 0) where the axes cross
Read the x-coordinate (first number): move right that many units
Read the y-coordinate (second number): move up that many units
Place a dot at that location and label it with the ordered pair
To read a point: follow left/down to find x, then down/left to find y

examples.title: Plotting (4, 3)
examples.text: Start at origin. Move RIGHT 4 units on the x-axis. Then move UP 3 units. Place a dot and label it (4, 3). You are 4 over and 3 up!

examples.title: Reading a Point
examples.text: A point is located 2 units to the right and 5 units up from the origin. What are its coordinates? (2, 5). The x is always first!

lessons.tip: Remember: x comes before y in the alphabet, so x comes first in the ordered pair! Think of it as 'walk into the building first (x), then take the elevator up (y).' Over then up, every time!

quiz.q: To plot the point (5, 2), which direction do you move first?
quiz.explanation: The x-coordinate (5) comes first. Move RIGHT 5 units on the x-axis, then UP 2.

quiz.q: What are the coordinates of the origin?
quiz.explanation: The origin is where both axes meet, at (0, 0).

quiz.q: A point is 3 units right and 4 units up. What are its coordinates?
quiz.explanation: Right gives x=3, up gives y=4. The ordered pair is (3, 4).

lessons.title: Angle Measurement
lessons.description: Measure and classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, and straight.
lessons.formula:
Types of Angles:
Acute:    less than 90°  (a cute little angle)
Right:    exactly 90°   (like an L)
Obtuse:   more than 90° but less than 180°
Straight: exactly 180°  (a straight line)

A full circle = 360°
lessons.content:
An angle is formed when two rays meet at a point called the vertex. We measure angles in degrees (°) using a tool called a protractor. Angles are everywhere: the corner of a book is a right angle (90°), and scissors make an acute angle when partially open.

There are four main types of angles. An acute angle is less than 90° — think of it as a cute, small angle. A right angle is exactly 90° and looks like the letter L. An obtuse angle is bigger than 90° but less than 180°. A straight angle is exactly 180° and forms a straight line.
steps: Find the vertex (where the two rays meet)
Place the center of the protractor on the vertex
Align one ray with the zero line of the protractor
Read the number where the second ray crosses the scale
Classify: is it acute (<90°), right (=90°), obtuse (>90°), or straight (=180°)?

examples.title: Classifying Angles
examples.text: An angle measuring 45° is acute (less than 90°). An angle measuring 90° is a right angle. An angle measuring 120° is obtuse (more than 90°). An angle of 180° is straight.

examples.title: Estimating Angles
examples.text: Look at a door partly open — that angle looks about 45°, so it is acute. A book corner is exactly 90° (right angle). A clock at 6:00 makes a straight angle of 180°.

lessons.tip: To estimate angles without a protractor, use your right angle as a benchmark. Make an L shape with your thumb and index finger — that is 90°. If the angle is smaller than your L, it is acute. If it is bigger, it is obtuse!

quiz.q: An angle measures 35°. What type of angle is it?
quiz.explanation: 35° is less than 90°, so it is an acute angle.

quiz.q: What is a right angle measured in degrees?
quiz.explanation: A right angle is always exactly 90°.

quiz.q: An angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle. What type is it?
quiz.explanation: An obtuse angle is greater than 90° but less than 180°.

lessons.title: Symmetry
lessons.description: Identify lines of symmetry in 2D shapes and create symmetrical figures.
lessons.formula:
Lines of Symmetry:
Square: 4 lines of symmetry
Rectangle: 2 lines of symmetry
Equilateral Triangle: 3 lines
Circle: infinite lines of symmetry

A shape is symmetrical if you can fold it
along a line and both halves match exactly.
lessons.content:
Symmetry is when a shape can be folded along a line and both halves match perfectly, like a mirror image. This line is called a line of symmetry. For example, if you fold a butterfly in half vertically, both wings match — the body is the line of symmetry.

Different shapes have different numbers of symmetry lines. A square has 4 lines of symmetry (vertical, horizontal, and two diagonals). A rectangle has only 2 (vertical and horizontal). An equilateral triangle has 3. A circle has infinite lines of symmetry because every diameter divides it into matching halves. Not all shapes have symmetry — a parallelogram has zero lines of symmetry!
steps: Look at the shape and imagine folding it in half
Try folding vertically (top to bottom): do both sides match?
Try folding horizontally (left to right): do both sides match?
Try folding along the diagonals: do both sides match?
Count all the lines where the fold creates a perfect match

examples.title: Does a Heart Have Symmetry?
examples.text: Yes! A heart shape has 1 vertical line of symmetry down the center. Fold it in half top to bottom and both sides match perfectly.

examples.title: Lines of Symmetry in a Square
examples.text: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: one vertical down the center, one horizontal across the middle, and two diagonals from corner to corner.

lessons.tip: To check for symmetry quickly, use a small mirror! Place the mirror along a possible line of symmetry. If the reflection looks exactly like the real shape, you found a line of symmetry. This is a great hands-on way to explore!

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have?
quiz.explanation: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry: vertical and horizontal through the center.

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
quiz.explanation: A circle can be folded along any diameter, so it has infinite lines of symmetry.

quiz.q: Which letter has a vertical line of symmetry?
quiz.explanation: The letter A has one vertical line of symmetry down its center. If you fold it in half, both sides match.

lessons.title: Customary and Metric Unit Conversions
lessons.description: Learn how to convert measurements within the customary system (inches, feet, miles) and the metric system (centimeters, meters, kilometers) by multiplying or dividing.
lessons.formula:
Customary Conversions:
1 foot = 12 inches
1 yard = 3 feet
1 mile = 5,280 feet

Metric Conversions:
1 meter = 100 centimeters
1 kilometer = 1,000 meters
1 liter = 1,000 milliliters
lessons.content:
Measurement is all around us, and different situations call for different units. In the United States, people commonly use the customary system with units like inches, feet, yards, and miles for length, while most of the world uses the metric system with centimeters, meters, and kilometers. Converting between units within the same system is a practical skill you will use in cooking, building, sports, and science.

The key to unit conversion is knowing your conversion factors — the fixed amounts that tell you how many smaller units equal one larger unit. When converting from a larger unit to a smaller unit (such as feet to inches), you multiply because there are more of the smaller units. When converting from a smaller unit to a larger unit (such as inches to feet), you divide because there are fewer of the larger units. For example, to convert 5 feet to inches, multiply 5 by 12 to get 60 inches; to convert 48 inches to feet, divide 48 by 12 to get 4 feet.

The metric system is especially easy to work with because it is based on powers of ten. Moving from meters to centimeters requires multiplying by 100, and moving from centimeters to meters requires dividing by 100. The prefixes milli- (thousandth), centi- (hundredth), and kilo- (thousand) tell you exactly how to shift the decimal point. Whether you are measuring a bookshelf in centimeters or planning a road trip in kilometers, understanding these conversions gives you confidence and accuracy.
steps: Identify the unit you are starting with and the unit you want to convert to.
Determine whether you are converting to a larger unit (divide) or a smaller unit (multiply).
Find the correct conversion factor for those two units.
Set up your calculation: multiply when going to smaller units, divide when going to larger units.
Solve and check your answer by converting back using the opposite operation.

examples.title: Converting 7 Feet to Inches
examples.text: We are converting from a larger unit (feet) to a smaller unit (inches), so we multiply. The conversion factor is 1 foot = 12 inches. Multiply 7 by 12: 7 × 12 = 84. So 7 feet equals 84 inches.

examples.title: Converting 350 Centimeters to Meters
examples.text: We are converting from a smaller unit (centimeters) to a larger unit (meters), so we divide. The conversion factor is 1 meter = 100 centimeters. Divide 350 by 100: 350 ÷ 100 = 3.5. So 350 centimeters equals 3.5 meters.

lessons.tip: Use the mnemonic "King Henry Died By Drinking Chocolate Milk" to remember metric prefixes in order: Kilo, Hecto, Deca, Base, Deci, Centi, Milli. Each step left divides by 10; each step right multiplies by 10.

quiz.q: How many inches are in 4 feet?
quiz.explanation: Since 1 foot = 12 inches, multiply 4 by 12 to get 48 inches.

quiz.q: How many meters are in 500 centimeters?
quiz.explanation: Since 1 meter = 100 centimeters, divide 500 by 100 to get 5 meters.

quiz.q: If a ribbon is 2 yards long, how many feet is it?
quiz.explanation: Since 1 yard = 3 feet, multiply 2 by 3 to get 6 feet.

quiz.q: How many milliliters are in 3 liters?
quiz.explanation: Since 1 liter = 1,000 milliliters, multiply 3 by 1,000 to get 3,000 milliliters.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Word Problems with All Four Operations
lessons.description: Tackle complex word problems that require two or more operations, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, by breaking them into manageable steps.
lessons.formula:
Steps to Solve Multi-Step Problems:

1. Read the entire problem carefully.
2. Identify the hidden questions you must answer first.
3. Choose the correct operations and solve each step.
4. Check your answer against the original question.
lessons.content:
Many real-world math problems cannot be solved with a single calculation. A multi-step word problem requires you to perform two or more operations — such as addition followed by multiplication, or division followed by subtraction — to arrive at the final answer. The challenge is figuring out which steps to take and in what order, which is why developing a clear strategy is so important.

The most common mistake students make is grabbing numbers and computing without truly understanding what the problem is asking. To avoid this, start by reading the entire problem carefully and asking yourself: what is the hidden question? A hidden question is a piece of information you must find before you can answer the main question. For example, if a problem asks how much money is left after buying multiple items at different prices, the hidden question might be finding the total cost of all items before subtracting from the starting amount.

After identifying all the steps, choose the correct operations for each step. Keywords like "in all" and "altogether" often signal addition or multiplication, while "how many more" and "remaining" often signal subtraction or division. Write out each step clearly, show your work, and always check your final answer by rereading the original problem to make sure your answer makes sense. With practice, you will learn to see the structure behind even the most complicated word problems.
steps: Read the entire problem at least twice to understand the scenario and what is being asked.
Identify the hidden question or questions that must be answered before the main question.
Decide which operation (add, subtract, multiply, or divide) to use for each step.
Solve each step in order, writing down your calculations as you go.
Check your final answer by rereading the problem and verifying that your answer is reasonable.

examples.title: Classroom Party Supplies
examples.text: Ms. Garcia buys 4 packs of juice boxes with 6 boxes in each pack. Each pack costs $3. She also buys 3 bags of chips at $2 each. She pays with a $50 bill. How much change does she get? Cost of juice: 4 × $3 = $12. Cost of chips: 3 × $2 = $6. Total spent: $12 + $6 = $18. Change: $50 − $18 = $32.

examples.title: Library Book Distribution
examples.text: A library has 240 books to distribute equally among 6 classrooms. After distribution, each classroom gives away 5 books to students who move. How many books does each classroom keep? First, divide: 240 ÷ 6 = 40 books per classroom. Then subtract: 40 − 5 = 35. Each classroom keeps 35 books.

lessons.tip: Circle the numbers and underline the question in the word problem. This simple habit helps you focus on what information you have and what you need to find, making it much easier to plan your steps.

quiz.q: A bakery makes 12 boxes of cookies with 24 cookies in each box. They sell 180 cookies. How many cookies are left?
quiz.explanation: First find the total: 12 × 24 = 288 cookies. Then subtract the sold cookies: 288 − 180 = 108 cookies left.

quiz.q: Maria has $45. She buys 3 notebooks that cost $4 each and a pen that costs $3. How much money does she have left?
quiz.explanation: Cost of notebooks: 3 × $4 = $12. Total spent: $12 + $3 = $15. Money left: $45 − $15 = $30.

quiz.q: A farmer has 5 fields with 36 apple trees in each field. He picks 8 apples from each tree and packs them into bags of 12. How many bags does he fill?
quiz.explanation: Total trees: 5 × 36 = 180 trees. Total apples: 180 × 8 = 1,440 apples. Bags: 1,440 ÷ 12 = 120 bags.

quiz.q: A school has 3 grade levels with 4 classes each. Each class has 28 students. If 56 students join the school, what is the new total?
quiz.explanation: Total classes: 3 × 4 = 12 classes. Total students: 12 × 28 = 336 students. After 56 join: 336 + 56 = 392 students.
